title: Common intention vs common object - a frequently confused distinction
p1:
Two legal phrases sound almost identical… but they can lead to very different consequences.

Many people confuse “common intention” with “common object” and assume they mean the same thing. They don’t.
p2:
The surprising difference is this: common intention is about a shared plan between people to commit a particular act. Common object is about a shared purpose of a group, even if every person did not plan each individual action.

For example, if two people agree beforehand to commit an offence and act together, common intention may become relevant. But when a group gathers with a shared unlawful purpose, the law may examine their common object.
p3:
A simple way to remember it: intention focuses on the meeting of minds between individuals, while object focuses on the purpose of the group.

This small distinction can completely change how liability is examined in a criminal case. Knowing the difference helps avoid a very common misunderstanding about group offences.
conclusion: Have you come across a situation where people in a group were held responsible differently despite not having the same level of involvement?
